summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for managing DS3 and E3 interfaces, which are high-speed digital line types used in telephone and carrier networks. It is a companion to other interface MIB documents.

plainLanguage.summary: DS3 and E3 are the wide-area digital carrier links that carry a whole digital hierarchy on one pair of wires. This RFC defines the SNMP objects that let a manager watch and configure such an interface: its type, its state, its error counters and its loopback settings. It is a companion to the MIBs for the smaller interface types.

subtitle: The SNMP objects for watching and configuring DS3 and E3 carrier interfaces.

tldr.problem: DS3 and E3 links carry a whole digital hierarchy over one pair of wires, and their fault and performance behaviour is defined in detail by the standards, but there was no standard set of SNMP objects for managing them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DS3-MIB module at transmission 30, with configuration, current, interval and total tables for the local and far ends. It covers line type, line status as a bit map, transmit clock source, channelization, loopbacks and the error and performance counters.
tldr.outcome: A manager can configure a DS3/E3 interface and read its error and performance history in the same terms the standards use. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2496 and is a companion to the DS0, DS1/E1/DS2/E2 and SONET/SDH MIBs.

today: RFC 3896 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004. It obsoletes RFC 2496, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Framework and What Changed
sections.content:
Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base or MIB, and are generally accessed through SNMP. The RFC specifies a MIB module compliant to SMIv2, described in STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580, and points readers to Section 7 of RFC 3410 for a detailed overview of the documents that describe the current Internet-Standard Management Framework.

Section 1.1 lists the changes from RFC 2496. The dsx3FracIfIndex SYNTAX now matches the described range, a reference to the Circuit Identifier object was added, the section on the use of ifStackTable was updated, the DESCRIPTION clauses of a few statistic objects were aligned with the near end and far end definitions and with RFC 3593, and a new value, dsx3M13, was added to dsx3LineType.

Section 1.2 lists the larger changes from RFC 1407: the Fractional Table has been deprecated, the document uses SMIv2, values are given for ifTable and ifXTable, an example of ifStackTable use is included, dsx3IfIndex has been deprecated, the definition of valid intervals was clarified for the case where the agent proxies for other devices, an inward loopback was added, further lineStatus bits were added for Near End in Unavailable Signal State and Carrier Equipment Out of Service, a read-write line Length object was added, a lineStatus last change, trap and enabler were added, textual conventions for statistics objects were used, a new dsx3LoopbackStatus object was introduced to reflect the loopbacks actually established while dsx3LoopbackConfig continues to hold the desired state, a dual loopback was added so an inward loopback and a line loopback can be set at the same time, an object was added to indicate whether the interface is channelized, and a new object indicates which DS1 is to be set for a remote loopback.

Section 1.3 names the companion documents: the MIBs for the DS0 (RFC 2494), DS1/E1/DS2/E2 (RFC 3895) and SONET/SDH (RFC 3592) interface types.
sections.plainLanguage: DS3 and E3 are the wide-area digital carrier links that carry a whole digital hierarchy on one pair of wires. This RFC defines the SNMP objects that let a manager watch and configure such an interface: its type, its state, its error counters and its loopback settings. It is a companion to the MIBs for the smaller interface types.

sections.title: What the Module Covers
sections.content:
These objects are used when the media realizing an interface is a DS3 or E3 interface. At present this applies to the value ds3 (30) of the ifType variable in the Internet-standard MIB.

The DS3 definitions are based on the DS3 specifications in ANSI T1.102-1987, ANSI T1.107-1988, ANSI T1.107a-1990 and ANSI T1.404-1989. The E3 definitions are based on the E3 specifications in CCITT G.751 and ETSI T/NA(91)18.

Section 2.1 gives the values that the standard ifTable should hold for a DS3 layer. Only the ifGeneralInformationGroup needs to be supported. ifType is ds3(30). ifSpeed is the speed of the line rate: 44736000 for DS3 and 34368000 for E3. ifPhysAddress holds the value of the Circuit Identifier, and if no Circuit Identifier has been assigned it should have a zero-length octet string. ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable is set to enabled(1). ifHighSpeed is the speed of the line in megabits per second, either 45 or 34. ifConnectorPresent is set to true(1) normally, except in cases such as DS3 over AAL1/ATM where false(2) is appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB applies to interfaces whose ifType is ds3, value 30. The DS3 definitions are based on the ANSI T1.102, T1.107 and T1.404 standards, and the E3 definitions on CCITT G.751 and ETSI T/NA(91)18. A DS3 line runs at 44.736 Mbit/s and an E3 line at 34.368 Mbit/s.

sections.title: Stacking, Channelizing and Loopbacks
sections.content:
Section 2.2 gives the usage guidelines that a manager needs in order to read the objects correctly.

The object dsx3IfIndex has been deprecated. It previously allowed a very special proxy situation for routers and channel service units, and the section now describes how to use ifStackTable to represent that relationship instead. The ifStackTable is used in the proxy case to represent the association between pairs of interfaces, for example that this DS3 is attached to that DS3. The RFC says this use is consistent with the table's usual purpose of showing the association between sub-layers of an interface: in both cases entire PDUs are exchanged between the interface pairs, whole DS3 frames in the case of a DS3 and whole HDLC frames in the case of PPP and HDLC. It is not meant to suggest using the table to represent time division multiplexing connections in general.

The RFC's worked example is a shelf of channel service units connected to a router, with an SNMP agent on the router that proxies for itself and for the units, and with an Ethernet interface on the router as well. The agent numbers the interfaces so that the four router-side DS3 interfaces come first, then the four CSU router-side interfaces, then the four CSU network-side interfaces, and it fills the ifStackTable so that each router interface points at the matching CSU router interface, and each of those at the matching CSU network interface. The RFC also gives the variant where the shelf is managed by its own local agent, in which case the Ethernet and router interfaces are deleted and the interfaces are numbered from 1 to 8.

Channelization is described next. Assume a DS3 with ifIndex 1 is channelized into DS1s without DS2s, and that dsx3Channelization is set to enabledDs1. Then 28 ifEntries of type DS1 are created by the agent, with ifIndex values 2 to 29 in channel order, and the DS1 MIB has an entry in dsx1ChanMappingTable for each DS1, mapping the DS3's ifIndex and channel number to the mapped ifIndex. Setting dsx3Channelization to disabled destroys the DS1s again. A DS3 channelized into DS2s uses enabledDs2 and creates 7 DS2s.

Loopbacks are covered in Section 2.2.4, and the objects that support them include dsx3LoopbackConfig for the desired state and dsx3LoopbackStatus for the loopbacks actually established, together with the source of the requests. A dual loopback allows an inward loopback and a line loopback to be set at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: Three usage rules matter in practice. A proxy that manages both a router and the line terminating equipment behind it uses the standard ifStackTable to record which router interface sits above which line interface, so the old special-purpose index object is no longer needed. Setting the channelization object makes the agent create or delete the smaller interfaces inside the line. And the loopback objects let a manager send the signal back towards itself, either locally or at the far end.

sections.title: Error Events
sections.content:
Section 2.4 of the RFC defines the terms the counters are built from. Section 2.4.1 covers the error events.

A Bipolar Violation (BPV) error event, for B3ZS or HDB3 coded signals, is the occurrence of a pulse of the same polarity as the previous pulse without being part of the zero substitution code. For B3ZS coded signals it may also include other error patterns such as three or more consecutive zeros and incorrect polarity.

An Excessive Zeros (EXZ) error event is the occurrence of any zero string length equal to or greater than 3 for B3ZS, or greater than 4 for HDB3.

A Line Coding Violation (LCV) error event is a count of both BPVs and EXZs occurring over the accumulation period. An EXZ increments the LCV by one regardless of the length of the zero string. It is also known as CV-L.

A P-bit Coding Violation (PCV) error event is, for all DS3 applications, a P-bit Parity Error event: the occurrence of a received P-bit code on the DS3 M-frame that is not identical to the corresponding locally calculated code.

A C-bit Coding Violation (CCV) error event is, for C-bit Parity and SYNTRAN DS3 applications, the count of coding violations reported via the C-bits. For C-bit Parity it is a count of CP-bit parity errors occurring in the accumulation interval, and for SYNTRAN it is a count of CRC-9 errors occurring in the accumulation interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters are defined in terms of specific faults in the signal. A bipolar violation is a pulse of the same polarity as the one before it. Excessive zeros is a run of zeros longer than the coding allows. A line coding violation counts both of those. A P-bit coding violation is a received parity bit that does not match the one the receiver calculated, and a C-bit coding violation is the same idea for the C-bits.

sections.title: Performance Parameters
sections.content:
All performance parameters are accumulated in fifteen minute intervals, and up to 96 intervals, a day's worth, are kept by an agent. Fewer than 96 intervals of data will be available if the agent has been restarted within the last 24 hours. In addition there is a rolling 24-hour total of each performance parameter. There is no requirement for an agent to fix the relationship between the start of an interval and any wall clock, though some agents align the intervals with quarter hours.

The performance parameters are of the types PerfCurrentCount, PerfIntervalCount and PerfTotalCount. All of these textual conventions are Gauge32, and they are used because it is possible for these objects to decrease: objects may decrease when Unavailable Seconds occurs across a fifteen minute interval boundary.

The counters are defined as follows. A Line Errored Second (LES) is a second in which one or more CV occurred or one or more LOS defects, also known as ES-L. A P-bit Errored Second (PES) is a second with one or more PCVs, or one or more Out of Frame defects, or a detected incoming AIS; this gauge is not incremented when UASs are counted, and it is also known as ESP-P. A P-bit Severely Errored Second (PSES) is a second with 44 or more PCVs, or one or more Out of Frame defects, or a detected incoming AIS, and it is also known as SESP-P. A C-bit Errored Second (CES) and a C-bit Severely Errored Second (CSES) are the same idea for the C-bits, with 44 or more CCVs for the severe case, and they apply only to the SYNTRAN and C-bit Parity DS3 applications. A Severely Errored Framing Second (SEFS) is a second with one or more Out of Frame defects or a detected incoming AIS, and it is not incremented during unavailable seconds.

Unavailable Seconds (UAS) are calculated by counting the number of seconds that the interface is unavailable. The DS3 interface is said to be unavailable from the onset of 10 contiguous PSESs, or the onset of the condition leading to a failure. If that condition was immediately preceded by one or more contiguous PSESs, the unavailability starts from the onset of those PSESs. Once unavailable, and if no failure is present, the interface becomes available at the onset of 10 contiguous seconds with no PSESs; if a failure is present, the same applies when the failure clearing time is at most 10 seconds, and otherwise the interface becomes available at the onset of 10 contiguous seconds with no PSESs or the onset period leading to the successful clearing condition, whichever occurs later.

With respect to the DS3 error counts, all counters are incremented while the interface is deemed available, and while it is deemed unavailable the only count incremented is UASs. The RFC points out the consequence: the agent cannot determine until after a ten second interval has passed whether a given one-second interval belongs to available or unavailable time, so an agent that updates the statistics in real time must be prepared to retroactively reduce the PES, PSES, CES and CSES counts by 10 and increase the UAS count by 10 when it determines that available time has been entered, and to adjust the PCV, CCV and SEFS counts as necessary, since those parameters are not accumulated during unavailable time.
sections.plainLanguage: All the counters are gathered in fifteen-minute intervals, and an agent keeps up to 96 of them, a full day, plus a rolling 24-hour total. The counts are gauges rather than counters because a second can move from available to unavailable after the fact, so the values can go down as well as up.

sections.title: The Objects and Their Tables
sections.content:
The module is named DS3-MIB and is placed at transmission 30. It defines a configuration table and then, for both the local end and the far end, a table of statistics for the current interval, a table of statistics for past intervals and a table of totals.

The configuration table holds the settings an operator can change. dsx3LineType says which application the interface is running, and its type affects how the usage and error statistics should be read: the values are dsx3other(1), dsx3M23(2), dsx3SYNTRAN(3), dsx3CbitParity(4), dsx3ClearChannel(5), e3other(6), e3Framed(7), e3Plcp(8) and dsx3M13(9), the last of which was added by this revision. The rate of DS3 is 44.736 Mbps and of E3 34.368 Mbps, and the dsx3ClearChannel value means that the C-bits are not used except for sending and receiving AIS.

dsx3LineStatus is a bit map, with the syntax INTEGER (1..4095), so it can show several failures and a loopback at the same time. The dsx3NoAlarm bit must be set if and only if no other flag is set. The bit positions are 1 dsx3NoAlarm, 2 dsx3RcvRAIFailure, 4 dsx3XmitRAIAlarm, 8 dsx3RcvAIS, 16 dsx3XmitAIS, 32 dsx3LOF, 64 dsx3LOS, 128 dsx3LoopbackState, 256 dsx3RcvTestCode, 512 dsx3OtherFailure, 1024 dsx3UnavailSigState and 2048 dsx3NetEquipOOS. If the loopback state bit is set, the loopback in effect can be determined from the dsx3LoopbackConfig object.

Other configuration objects include dsx3TransmitClockSource, whose values are loopTiming(1) for the recovered receive clock, localTiming(2) for a local or external clock, and throughTiming(3) for a clock derived from the recovered receive clock of another DS3 interface; dsx3InvalidIntervals, the number of intervals with no data available; and dsx3LineLength, the length of the line in metres, with the range 0 to 64000, which can be used by line build out circuitry. dsx3Channelization says whether the interface is channelized, with the values disabled(1), enabledDs1(2) and enabledDs2(3), and setting it causes the creation or deletion of the corresponding entries in the ifTable. dsx3Ds1ForRemoteLoop, with the range 0 to 29, says which DS1 or E1 on the interface will be indicated in a remote DS1 loopback request, where 0 means no DS1 will be looped and 29 means all of them will be.

The statistics tables use the textual conventions PerfCurrentCount, PerfIntervalCount and PerfTotalCount from the Performance History MIB of RFC 3593, all of which are Gauge32.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has a configuration table for the local end and another for the far end, and for each of those a table for the current interval, a table of past intervals and a table of totals. The configuration table holds the writable settings: the line type, the transmit clock source, the line length, the channelization, and the loopback mode. The status is a bit map, so several faults and a loopback can be reported at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that a number of management objects in this MIB module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write, and that such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

Setting the following objects to incorrect values may result in traffic interruptions: dsx3LineType, dsx3LineCoding, dsx3SendCode, dsx3LoopbackConfig, dsx3TransmitClockSource, dsx3LineLength, dsx3Channelization and dsx3Ds1ForRemoteLoop. The RFC gives two examples. In the case of dsx3LineType, both ends of a DS3/E3 must have the same value in order for traffic to flow. In the case of dsx3SendCode and dsx3LoopbackConfig, traffic may stop transmitting when particular loopbacks are applied.

Setting dsx3FarEndEquipCode, dsx3FarEndLocationIDCode, dsx3FarEndFrameIDCode, dsx3FarEndUnitCode or dsx3FarEndFacilityIDCode to an incorrect value will result in the remote end receiving an incorrect Path Identification message, which may result in a connectivity inconsistency.
sections.plainLanguage: Several objects can be written, and a wrong value can interrupt traffic or make the far end receive a wrong path identification. The RFC lists the sensitive ones and notes that allowing writes on a network without proper protection can hurt the network's operation.
